lead.kicker: TOP STORY  •  YEMEN AND SAUDI ARABIA
lead.headline: Missiles Hit Aden as Riyadh’s Airport Stays Shut
lead.deck: Saudi Arabia says 12 people died in the 10 October attack on Riyadh airport.
body: Yemen’s war has reached Saudi cities. The Houthis, who control Sanaa in Yemen, have been attacking Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s civil war reignited in July. On 10 October a strike hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia says 12 people were killed and 300 were wounded. The airport is still suspended, while Jeddah and Dammam are running with delays.

The fighting is also inside Yemen. On Thursday 15 October, Houthi missiles hit the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden, the government’s interim capital. Yemen’s health minister said five people were killed and 16 wounded. The UN Security Council condemned the Houthi attacks in a presidential statement, which Saudi Arabia welcomed.

Washington has not joined the fight. On Friday 16 October, Donald Trump said Saudi Arabia should accept help from Israel and that Saudi–Israeli ties could return to the agenda. Riyadh has said it will normalise relations only with a clear path to Palestinian statehood. Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging the Houthis; Iran denies it and has offered to mediate.
The effects reach well beyond the region. Air India suspended flights to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until 20 October, and IndiGo suspended several Saudi routes until 24 October.

Saudi forces are fighting back. The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu, two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and drones elsewhere, and destroyed Houthi storage sites in Sanaa, Saada and Amran.

world.headline: Oil Tops $110 and Tech Shares Fall
world.deck: Brent crude closed at $109.86 a barrel on Friday as the Hormuz disruption continued.
body: Think of the Strait of Hormuz as the only narrow door out of a huge warehouse. Before the war, nearly a fifth of the world’s oil passed through this waterway between Iran and its southern neighbours. The war began in late February when the US and Israel attacked Iran, and shipping there has been disrupted ever since.

On Friday 16 October, Brent crude, the benchmark price for oil, briefly topped $110 a barrel, its highest since May, and closed at $109.86. The price rose 4.9% over the week. UKMTO, which tracks ship incidents, recorded 12 vessel attacks in the past week, 10 of them in the Strait of Hormuz. US crude, called WTI, rose 3.5% to close at $101.41.

The shock spread to share markets. Technology companies lost more than $1 trillion in value on Friday. One reason given is that higher fuel prices push up inflation, which makes higher interest rates more likely. Iran’s army chief says the strait remains closed; US Central Command says 400 commercial vessels passed through in the past week.

Two other forces are at work. A report says Ukrainian attacks have shut down much of Russia’s refining capacity, which also tightens supply. And on 14 October the container ship GFS Pride sank in the Hormuz area after being hit. Oman warned ships to avoid floating containers near Musandam.

Oil companies gained as tech shares fell. Exxon and Chevron each rose about 2.5% on Friday. Their costs are mostly fixed, so higher oil prices flow largely to profit. For technology firms, higher interest rates make future profits worth less today, which is one reason their shares fell.

Prices like these matter because the war and the strait are still unresolved. Iran’s army chief says the strait is closed, while US Central Command says traffic is moving, so the picture changes with each ship that is hit or passes safely.

uk.headline: Burnham Offers Scotland a Deal to Move Power Outward
uk.deck: The Prime Minister visited Lanarkshire on 16 October.
body: Devolution means a national government passing some of its powers to a smaller region. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who took office in July, has made it central to his agenda. On Friday 16 October he visited Lanarkshire in Scotland and offered to work with the Scottish Government on moving decisions to Scotland’s regions.

He called it an offer: “This is me making an offer to the Scottish Government.” The plan would use the No10 North initiative and the Scotland Office. The Scottish Government had already proposed replacing Scotland’s 32 councils with six to ten regional authorities and 120 to 160 community authorities.

Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander said power should not stop at the Scottish Parliament’s doors. Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth welcomed the visit. It came as the SNP held its national conference in Aberdeen, its first since winning the most seats at the May Holyrood election.
uk.why: Who holds power, in Westminster, Holyrood or local areas, decides who answers for schools, jobs and planning.
also: Iran: Mr Burnham said a plot against RAF Fairford was highly likely coordinated in Iran; Iran denies it and summoned Britain’s ambassador.
Fairford: Seven suspects were arrested on 27 September and bailed. No one has been charged.

europe.headline: EU Leaders Back Ukraine but Leave the Budget Unsettled
europe.deck: Zelenskyy asked for 70 billion euros more for next year.
body: EU leaders met in Brussels on 15 and 16 October. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the war will cost Ukraine 155 billion euros next year and asked for 70 billion euros more. The EU has already agreed a 90 billion euro loan for 2026 and 2027. The Commission was asked to propose how to close the gap, and leaders kept sanctions on Russia.

The summit also failed to settle the EU’s long-term budget for 2028 to 2034. The Commission proposed nearly 2 trillion euros. The Irish presidency’s compromise would cut about 141 billion euros, but Euronews reports that proposal is now dead. Six fiscally conservative countries led by Germany want a smaller budget. Seventeen “Friends of Cohesion”, including Italy and Spain, want to protect farm and regional funds.

European Council President António Costa is expected to present a compromise before a special summit on 26 November. Leaders also asked the Commission for a toolbox of trade defences against China. The EU’s trade deficit with China is about 360 billion euros, and Chinese exports to the EU rose 25% over the past year.

lead.headline: Yemen’s War Reaches Saudi Cities, and Missiles Hit Aden
body: Yemen has a civil war. That is a war between groups inside one country. It started again in July. A group called the Houthis controls Sanaa, a city in Yemen. Since July, the Houthis have been attacking Saudi Arabia.
On 10 October, a strike hit an airport in the Saudi city of Riyadh. Saudi Arabia says 12 people died. The airport is still shut.

The fighting is in Yemen too. On 15 October, Houthi missiles hit a palace in Aden. Yemen’s government is based in Aden for now. Five people were killed. The UN Security Council said the Houthi attacks were wrong.
Saudi Arabia says Iran is encouraging the Houthis. Iran denies this. Saudi-led forces say they have stopped missiles and drones. Some airlines have paused flights to Saudi cities.

world.headline: Oil Price Briefly Tops $110 as Tech Shares Fall
body: A lot of the world’s oil travels through the Strait of Hormuz. A strait is a narrow strip of sea. This one lies next to Iran. A war began in late February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran. Since then, shipping there has been disrupted. Some ships have been attacked.
On Friday 16 October, the price of oil briefly went above $110 a barrel. That was the highest price since May.

Share prices of technology companies fell. A share is a small part of a company that people can buy. Tech companies lost more than $1 trillion in value on Friday. One reason is that dearer fuel can push other prices up. That can lead to higher interest rates. Oil companies such as Exxon and Chevron gained.
Iran’s army chief says the strait is closed. But US Central Command says 400 ships passed through in the past week.

uk.headline: Prime Minister Offers to Help Scotland Give Its Regions More Power
body: Andy Burnham is the UK’s Prime Minister. He took office in July. He wants to move power outward. This is called devolution. It means a national government passes some of its powers to a smaller region.

On Friday 16 October, he visited Lanarkshire in Scotland. He offered to work with the Scottish Government. Together, they could move some decisions to Scotland’s regions. “This is me making an offer to the Scottish Government,” he said.

The Scottish Government already has its own idea. Scotland now has 32 councils, which are local governments. It has suggested replacing them with six to ten regional ones, plus smaller community ones.
Scotland’s Deputy First Minister, Jenny Gilruth, welcomed the visit. It came during the national conference of the SNP, a political party. The SNP won the most seats in Scotland’s election in May.

europe.headline: EU Leaders Back Ukraine but Cannot Agree on a Long-Term Budget
body: Leaders of EU countries met in Brussels on 15 and 16 October. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the war will cost Ukraine 155 billion euros next year. He asked for 70 billion euros more.

The EU has already agreed to lend Ukraine 90 billion euros. The leaders asked the European Commission to suggest how to close the gap. They also kept sanctions on Russia. Sanctions are punishments, such as limits on trade.

The leaders did not agree on the EU’s budget for 2028 to 2034. A budget is a plan for spending money. Some countries, led by Germany, want a smaller budget. Others, including Italy and Spain, want to protect money for farms and regions. Leaders will meet again at a special summit on 26 November.
